Other scripts · 2010–2019

Computers can crack a script, if they know a related language

Snyder, Barzilay and Knight 2010; Luo, Cao and Barzilay 2019 · ACL 2010; ACL 2019

In a sentence

Ugaritic and Linear B were re-deciphered by machine, but only by matching them to Hebrew and Greek.

In plain words

Machine learning re-cracked two ancient scripts: Ugaritic, matched against Hebrew, and Linear B, matched against early Greek. The trick only works when you already know a closely related language. For the Indus script, no such language is known.

Technical detail

Snyder et al. 2010: 29 of 30 Ugaritic letters recovered via Hebrew cognates. Luo et al. 2019: 67.3% of Linear B cognates recovered via Greek. Luo et al. 2021 found no strong evidence that Basque is related to Iberian.

How we read it

Read: full text. Sources opened: aclanthology.org/P10-1107.pdf, arxiv.org/pdf/1906.06718, aclanthology.org/2021.tacl-1.5.pdf.

What they did

  • Snyder, Barzilay and Knight (2010) built a Bayesian model that, given Ugaritic texts and a non-parallel Hebrew corpus, learns both the letter mapping and which Ugaritic words have which Hebrew cognates.
  • Their model used a Hebrew morphological lexicon with part-of-speech classes and allowed affixes taken from an annotated Hebrew Bible.
  • Luo, Cao and Barzilay (2019) replaced this with a neural sequence-to-sequence model of character correspondences, trained by casting word matching as a minimum-cost flow problem.
  • Luo et al. 2019 tested on Ugaritic-Hebrew, on Linear B against Greek cognates, and on Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.
  • Luo, Hartmann, Santus, Cao and Barzilay (2021) extended the method to texts without word boundaries and with no assumed related language, adding a language-closeness score, and tried it on Gothic, Ugaritic and Iberian.

What they found

  • Snyder et al. map 29 of 30 Ugaritic letters correctly (96.67%), against 22 of 30 for an HMM cipher baseline (section 8).
  • They translate 60.42% of Ugaritic word types that have Hebrew cognates, 66.71% by token, and 75.07% of morphemes by type (Table 1); Hebrew cognates exist for 2,155 word forms, about a third of the vocabulary (section 7.1).
  • Luo et al. 2019 identify 65.9% of Ugaritic cognates in the noisy setting against 60.4% for Snyder et al., and 93.5% in the noiseless setting (Table 2).
  • On Linear B they reach 84.7% on a 919-pair cognate list and 67.3% on the harder Linear B/names set (Table 3).
  • Removing the monotonic alignment or residual connection drops Ugaritic accuracy to 0%, and removing the flow training drops it to 8.6% (Table 5), so linguistic priors carry the result.
  • Luo et al. 2021 find their closeness measure picks the right relatives for Gothic and Ugaritic but shows no strong evidence that Basque is related to Iberian (abstract; Conclusions).

Strengths and limits

  • These are real, reproducible successes, with code and data released.
  • Every success assumes the lost script’s sign inventory is a small, segmental or syllabic set and that a large share of words have cognates in a known lexicon; the Linear B test uses a curated cognate list where every word has a match.
  • Iberian worked as a test only because its script is already phonetically readable; the Indus case lacks both sound values and a known relative.
  • The project’s cognate_decipher run already showed that with a realistic lexicon (only some words having cognates) recovery falls to about 1-39%.

What the authors say comes next

  • Use the known frequency of Hebrew words and morphemes, which the 2010 model ignores and which causes its commonest error. (Snyder et al. 2010, section 9)
  • Use literary context, not just vocabulary-level matching, since many words can only be deciphered in context. (Snyder et al. 2010, section 9)
  • Explore the model’s predictive power when the family of the lost language is unknown. (Snyder et al. 2010, section 9)
  • Use phonetic values inferred from cognate mappings as a starting point for reconstructing lost sounds; more work is needed to test this. (Luo et al. 2021, Conclusions)
  • Extend the method from language pairs to many languages at once. (Luo et al. 2021, Conclusions)

Ideas it gives us

  • Run the Luo 2021 language-closeness score as a pure negative-control bench: plant a logo-syllabic Dravidian-like and an Indo-Aryan-like text at Indus size and length, and measure whether the closeness score can tell the two apart when sound values are unknown. If it cannot separate planted families even in the ideal case, the ‘which family’ question is closed for this method at Indus size; if it can, it gives a calibrated tool. Open data enough: yes. Needs: DecipherUnsegmented code (released, licence to check), Tamil and Sanskrit word lists, the project’s planting code in cognate_decipher.
  • Apply the cognate machinery only to the foreign-found Gulf round-seal texts that break Indus order, matched against a list of Dilmun and Meluhha personal names from cuneiform. This is the one place where a related lexicon of names plausibly exists, and name lists are what the methods matched best (Linear B/names, 67.3%). Power is low (atlas 1.10 used n = 12), so it belongs with the existing crib_attack work rather than as a new route. Open data enough: no. Needs: A clean list of non-Sumerian, non-Akkadian names from Dilmun and Meluhha-linked tablets; partly in sealing_hunt and elamite_names, but small.

What we take from it

Closed

We tested the planted-language version at Indus size. Without the right language, it fails, so this route waits for an outside clue.

Read our result in the repository.
